unit.title: Protect self against communicable diseases in the workplace

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a communicable disease?
options: A disease that you are born with and cannot pass to others
An illness that can spread from one person to another
A disease caused only by eating too much sugar and salt
An illness caused by working long hours

questions.stem: A person carries a germ and can pass it on, but shows no signs of being ill. What is this person called?
options: A patient

A vector
A carrier

To stop the waste from drying out

questions.stem: What is the difference between 'isolation' and 'quarantine'?
options: Isolation is for sick people; quarantine is for people who may have caught it

options: So that the salon can charge the client for it
So it is recorded and checked by a doctor

options: Hire only staff who say that they never get sick at all

essays.stem: Explain the main ways communicable diseases can spread in a salon or spa, with an example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Germs spread in several ways. They spread through the air in droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks close to others; the flu and colds spread like this. They spread by direct contact, when skin touches skin; scabies and impetigo can spread like this. They spread by indirect contact, when germs are left on objects such as towels, combs, door handles or tools and then picked up by the next person; ringworm and conjunctivitis can spread this way. They spread through blood, when infected blood gets into a cut or the eyes, for example from a used blade; hepatitis B and HIV spread this way. They spread through food or water soiled with germs from faeces, often because of poor hand washing; hepatitis A and stomach bugs spread like this. Finally, vectors such as the Aedes mosquito spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika. Knowing the route helps staff choose the right way to stop it.
markingPoints: Droplets in the air, with an example such as flu
Direct skin contact, with an example such as scabies
Indirect contact through objects, with an example such as ringworm on towels
Blood, with an example such as hepatitis B or HIV
Food and water, or vectors such as mosquitoes, with an example

essays.stem: Describe the personal habits that help a therapist protect herself from catching communicable diseases at work.
essays.modelAnswer: She washes her hands often and properly, especially before and after each client, after touching used items, after the toilet and before eating. She keeps her nails short and clean and covers any cuts with a waterproof plaster. She wears gloves and other PPE when there is a risk of contact with blood, body fluids or broken skin. She avoids touching her eyes, nose and mouth with unwashed hands. She covers coughs and sneezes with a tissue or her elbow and puts the tissue in a bin. She uses her own cup, towel and other personal items and does not share them. She wears a clean uniform each day and ties long hair back. She keeps her vaccines up to date after talking to her doctor. She looks after her general health by eating well, drinking water, sleeping enough and managing stress, so that her body can fight infection. When she is ill she stays away from work and tells her supervisor.
markingPoints: Washes hands often and correctly, at the right times
Covers cuts and uses gloves and other PPE where there is a risk
Covers coughs and sneezes and does not touch her face
Does not share personal items, and wears a clean uniform each day
Keeps vaccines up to date, looks after her general health, and stays home when ill

essays.stem: Explain why vaccination is important for salon and spa workers, and name vaccines a worker should ask her doctor or health centre about.
essays.modelAnswer: A vaccine trains the body's immune system to recognise a germ, so that if the person meets it later, the body can fight it off before it causes serious illness. Salon and spa workers touch many clients each day, work close to people's faces and may come into contact with blood and broken skin, so they have a higher chance of meeting germs. Being vaccinated protects the worker, and it also helps protect clients, co-workers and family, because a protected person is less likely to pass the germ on. A worker should ask her doctor or the public health centre about the hepatitis B vaccine, because she may come into contact with blood from cuts or blades; about tetanus, which can get in through cuts; and about the yearly flu vaccine. The doctor may suggest others, such as those given in childhood, and will say how many doses are needed. She should keep a record of the vaccines she has had.
markingPoints: A vaccine trains the body to fight a germ before it causes illness
Salon workers are at higher risk through close contact and possible blood contact
Vaccination protects the worker and the people around her
Names hepatitis B, tetanus and flu
Asks a doctor or public health centre, and keeps a record

essays.stem: Describe what a worker should do straight after a cut from a used blade, or a splash of a client's blood into her eye or mouth.
essays.modelAnswer: For a cut, she lets the wound bleed gently, without sucking it or scrubbing it, and washes it well with soap and running water. Then she covers it with a waterproof dressing. For a splash in the eye, she rinses the eye straight away with plenty of clean running water or eyewash, without rubbing it. For a splash in the mouth, she spits it out and rinses her mouth with water several times, without swallowing. She must report what happened to her supervisor at once, even if she feels fine, and write it in the incident record, with the time, what happened and, if known, which client was involved. She should get medical advice quickly, the same day, from a doctor or hospital, because some treatments to prevent infection work best if they are started within hours. She should go back for any tests the doctor advises. The details are kept private.
markingPoints: Cut: lets it bleed, washes with soap and running water and covers it; no sucking or scrubbing
Eye or mouth: rinses at once with plenty of clean water; does not rub or swallow
Reports to the supervisor straight away and records the incident
Gets medical advice quickly, because early treatment works best
Follows up on tests, and the matter is kept confidential

essays.stem: Explain how staff can reduce the risk of dengue, chikungunya and Zika at and around the workplace.
essays.modelAnswer: These diseases are spread by the Aedes mosquito, which breeds in clean water left standing in containers and bites mostly in the daytime. At least once a week, staff can search the salon and the yard for anything that holds water, such as drums, buckets, old tyres, bottle caps, flower pot saucers, blocked gutters and plant holders, and empty, scrub, cover or throw them away. Water drums and tanks should have tight covers. Waste should be kept in bins with lids and collected regularly so that it does not hold rain water. Screens on windows and doors help keep mosquitoes out. Staff can use an insect repellent on bare skin, following the label, and wear light clothing that covers the arms and legs when outside. Anyone with a sudden fever, headache, joint or muscle pain, or a rash should see a doctor and not take medicines without advice. The salon should follow Ministry of Health and Wellness advice during an outbreak.
markingPoints: Knows the Aedes mosquito breeds in clean standing water and bites by day
Checks at least weekly and empties, covers or removes water containers
Keeps covers on drums and lids on bins, and uses screens
Uses repellent as the label says, and clothing that covers the skin
Sees a doctor with fever, pain or a rash, and follows Ministry of Health and Wellness advice

essays.topic: Coughs, colds and other airborne illness
essays.stem: A co-worker has had a cough and fever for two days. Explain what she should do, and how the rest of the staff can protect themselves.
essays.modelAnswer: The co-worker should not come to work while she has a fever. She should tell her supervisor as soon as possible, following the salon's sickness policy, and get advice from a doctor or health centre, especially if she has trouble breathing or the cough goes on for a long time. She should come back only when she is well, or when the policy or the doctor says she can. If she becomes ill at work, she should be sent home, cover her coughs, and wear a mask if she has to be near others. The rest of the staff can protect themselves by washing their hands often, not sharing cups or towels, keeping the salon well ventilated, and cleaning and disinfecting the surfaces that many people touch, such as door handles, phones and card machines, more often. They should watch for signs of illness in themselves and stay home if they become unwell. Everyone follows the Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance if there is an outbreak.
markingPoints: Stays home and tells the supervisor, following the sickness policy
Gets medical advice, especially if the illness is severe or lasts a long time
Returns only when well or when the policy allows; covers coughs or wears a mask near others
Others: hand washing, no sharing, good airflow, extra cleaning of surfaces many people touch
Others watch for symptoms and follow Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance

essays.stem: Explain how HIV is and is not spread, and how a workplace should treat a worker who is living with HIV.
essays.modelAnswer: HIV is spread through certain body fluids: blood, sexual fluids and breast milk. It can be passed on through sex without a condom, by sharing needles or other sharp items, from mother to baby, and by infected blood getting into a cut or the eyes, for example from a used blade at work. HIV is not spread by everyday contact. It is not passed on by shaking hands, hugging, sharing a toilet, cups or plates, by coughs or sneezes, or by mosquito bites. In a salon, staff stay safe by using standard precautions with every client, such as gloves, the sharps box and covered cuts. A worker who is living with HIV should be treated fairly and with respect, like anyone else. Her status is private and must not be shared without her permission. She must not be refused work, moved or bullied because of it. The workplace should have a written HIV policy, train its staff, and support the worker if she needs time off for medical care.
markingPoints: Spread through blood, sexual fluids and breast milk, including sharps and sex without a condom
Not spread by everyday contact, shared toilets or cups, or mosquitoes
Standard precautions protect staff at work
Her status is kept private; no discrimination or bullying
A written workplace HIV policy, staff training and support

essays.stem: Describe how staff should keep the staff room, food and drinking water safe, to prevent stomach illnesses.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff wash their hands with soap and water before they prepare or eat food and after they use the toilet. Food is kept covered, and food that can spoil, such as cooked rice, meat or milk products, goes into the fridge soon after it arrives instead of being left out for hours. Each person labels and dates their food and throws away old or out-of-date items. The fridge, microwave, tables and sink are cleaned regularly, and spills are wiped up at once. Cups, plates and cutlery are washed in hot, soapy water after use, and dishcloths are changed often. Waste goes into a bin with a lid that is emptied every day, so that flies, ants and rats are not attracted. Drinking water comes from a safe supply; when the authorities warn that the water may be unsafe, staff boil it and keep it covered, or use sealed bottled water. Salon chemicals are never stored with food, and anyone with diarrhoea or vomiting stays home.
markingPoints: Washes hands before handling food and after the toilet
Keeps food covered, chilled soon, labelled and dated
Cleans the fridge, surfaces and dishes regularly
Uses bins with lids, emptied daily, to keep pests away
Safe drinking water (boiled when advised), chemicals kept away from food, sick staff stay home

essays.stem: Explain the employer's and the worker's responsibilities for protecting workers from communicable diseases.
essays.modelAnswer: The employer must provide a safe workplace. This means having a written infection control and sickness policy that follows the Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance, training staff on it, and supplying enough soap, hand rub, paper towels, gloves, aprons and other PPE. The employer should provide sharps boxes, spill kits and safe waste collection, keep the salon clean and well ventilated, deal with pests, and give staff information about vaccines. The employer should allow sick workers to stay home and keep their health information private. The worker must follow the policy and the training, use the PPE provided correctly, wash her hands, cover her cuts, and keep her own vaccines up to date. She must report any injury, exposure, spill or hazard, such as a full sharps box or standing water, and she must tell her supervisor when she is ill and stay away from work. The two work together: the employer provides the means, and the worker uses them every time.
markingPoints: Employer: a written policy based on Ministry of Health and Wellness guidance, and training
Employer: supplies PPE, hand-washing items, sharps boxes and spill kits, and keeps the place clean and ventilated
Employer: supports sick workers and keeps health information private
Worker: follows the policy, uses PPE, and keeps up good hygiene and vaccines
Worker: reports injuries, hazards and illness

essays.stem: Explain the difference between bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, and give an example of an illness each one causes that could affect salon staff.
essays.modelAnswer: These are the main kinds of germs and organisms that cause communicable diseases. Bacteria are tiny living things made of a single cell. Many are harmless, but some cause illness, such as impetigo, boils and tuberculosis. A doctor can often treat a bacterial infection with antibiotics. Viruses are even smaller and can only multiply inside living cells. They cause illnesses such as colds, the flu, hepatitis B, HIV, cold sores and dengue. Antibiotics do not work against viruses. Fungi include moulds and yeasts. They like warm, damp places and cause infections such as athlete's foot, ringworm and fungal nail infections. Parasites live on or in another living thing and feed from it; examples are head lice and the scabies mite, which spread by close contact. Knowing the type of germ helps staff understand how an illness spreads and how to prevent it.
markingPoints: Bacteria: single cells; examples such as impetigo, boils or TB
Viruses: smaller and multiply inside cells; examples such as flu, hepatitis B or HIV
Fungi: like warm, damp places; examples such as athlete's foot or ringworm
Parasites: live on or in the body; examples such as head lice or scabies
Antibiotics treat bacteria but not viruses

practical1.title: Check the salon for communicable disease risks and make a staff action poster
practical1.brief: As a group, carry out a walk-through check of the Centre's salon or spa area, the staff room and the yard, using the risk checklist the assessor gives you. Look for anything that could help a communicable disease to spread, for example: containers holding water where mosquitoes could breed, bins without lids, uncovered food, shared cups or towels, an empty soap dispenser or hand rub, no paper towels, a sharps box that is too full, poor airflow, or surfaces that many hands touch and that need cleaning. Split the areas so that each member leads the check of one area while another member photographs it and a third writes it on the checklist. Put right at once only what is safe to put right (for example, empty and turn over a bucket, put a lid on a bin, refill the soap), and list the rest for the supervisor. Then, together, make an A3 poster for staff called 'Protect yourself at work', with at least six actions, each with a picture or drawing. Each member writes at least one section of the poster and explains it to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the completed checklist and the poster once for the whole group.
materials: The risk checklist from the assessor (one for each area)
Disposable gloves for moving containers or bins
Spare bin lids, soap and paper towels to put small problems right
A3 card or paper, markers, glue, and printed or drawn pictures
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The group with the blank checklists before starting
Each risk found, photographed where it was found (at least one for each member)
A risk being put right, for example a water container emptied and turned over
The completed checklist, with the list for the supervisor
The finished poster on the staff notice board
checklist: Took part in the walk-through and led the check of one area
Spotted real risks and said how each one could spread disease
Put right only what was safe to do, wearing gloves where needed
Wrote clear, accurate notes on the checklist
Wrote a correct section of the poster in plain words
Explained the section clearly to the assessor
Worked well with the group and shared the tasks
safety: Wear gloves when moving bins, containers or anything dirty, and wash your hands at the end
Do not open or empty a sharps box; report it to the supervisor
Do not touch rat droppings or dead pests; report them
Do not climb up to reach gutters or high places; report them instead

practical2.title: Hand hygiene, PPE and what to do after an exposure: a group drill
practical2.brief: As a group, show how you protect yourselves and what you do after an exposure. Stage 1: each member rubs a training lotion that shows up under an ultraviolet (UV) lamp onto their hands, washes their hands with soap and water, and checks them under the lamp while another member photographs the result and notes any missed areas. Stage 2: each member puts on a disposable apron, a mask, eye protection and gloves in the right order, then takes them off in the safe order without touching the outside of the gloves, and washes their hands. Stage 3: the assessor gives each pair a scenario card, for example a cut from a used blade, a client's blood splashed in the eye, or a co-worker who comes in with a fever. One member acts out the first aid or the action, using a clean dressing and miming any eye rinse (no real blood or sharps), while the other plays the supervisor. Then the pair fills in an incident report or a sickness note for that scenario. Each member takes each role once. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the reports and notes once for the whole group.
materials: A UV hand-hygiene training lotion and a UV lamp (used as the maker says)
A hand basin with liquid soap and paper towels
Disposable aprons, masks, eye protection, and nitrile gloves in several sizes
An eyewash bottle and waterproof plasters (for showing, not for use on eyes)
Incident report forms and sickness notes
A phone or camera for photos
photos: Each member's hands under the UV lamp after washing (hands only)
A member with full PPE on, put on in the right order
The gloves being taken off, inside out
Each scenario being acted out (hands or backs only)
The completed incident reports and sickness notes
checklist: Washed hands correctly and checked the result under the UV lamp
Put on PPE in the right order
Took off PPE safely, gloves first, without touching the outside, then washed hands
Gave the right first aid or action for the scenario
Reported to the 'supervisor' clearly and at once
Filled in the incident report or sickness note fully and accurately
Kept the scenario details private and spoke respectfully
safety: Do not look straight into the UV lamp; use it as the maker says
No real blood, needles or blades are used, and no water is put into anyone's eyes
Check for latex allergy; the Centre's gloves for this drill are nitrile
Put used PPE in the correct bin and wash hands at the end
